title: Training patterns, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medication use, and effects on high-altitude ultramarathon performance (Leadville Trail 100)
authors: Baldea JD, Khodaee M, Poddar SK, Hill JC, Johnson J
journal: ACSM 56th Annual Meeting, presentation 703 (abstract hosted by Coach Sci. Abstracts, San Diego State University)
population: Leadville Trail 100 (100 mi, 9,200-12,600 ft) entrants surveyed at registration; mean age 43.3 (21-71), 82.1% male.
findings: 351 of 444 entrants responded (79.1%); anonymous self-administered survey given at registration the day before the race.
Mean 5.2 training days per week; mean longest training run 51 miles; 51.7% trained from personal experience.

Altitude of residence, finishing goal, length of longest training run and training frequency per week had statistically significant relationships with finishing time; age, gender, arrival time, training duration, training altitude and NSAID use did not.
The abstract's implication line states these four variables 'correlated with a better finishing time'. No coefficients, and no finishing-rate or finisher-vs-DNF analysis, are given.
limitations: Conference abstract, not peer reviewed; self-reported longest run (likely includes races); no effect sizes; relates to finish time among respondents, not to finishing or injury; no DOI.
implications: Only a self-reported 100-mile entrant average (51 mi, far more than 6 h of running for most) with a direction (longer longest run, faster time); cannot support or refute a 6 h cap because race-distance runs inflate the figure.
Treat as descriptive context for what 100-mile entrants do, not as a dose-response for the engine.
